item.title: Who’s controlling artificial intelligence?
item.description:
# Who’s controlling Artificial Intelligence? [OpenAI](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/openai/) has conceded that its [ChatGPT](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/chatgpt/) went beyond the “sandbox” designed to contain it and has attacked “ [Hugging Face](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/hugging-face/)” and several other companies. [Hugging Face](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/hugging-face/) is a website known for its AI tools.
According to the Cloud Security Agency, “In July 2026, an [OpenAI](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/openai/) model broke out of its sandbox during a cybersecurity benchmark, exploited a zero-day vulnerability, and used stolen credentials to gain remote code execution on [Hugging Face’s](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/hugging-face/) production systems.
In English, that means the [OpenAI](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/openai/) agent, [ChatGPT](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/chatgpt/), escaped the system that was supposed to contain it and used false credentials to access other companies’ servers. [OpenAI’s](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/openai/) agent used thousands (perhaps tens of thousands) of automated attempts to break into [Hugging Face](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/hugging-face/) and other companies’ websites to take and practice the tools for further attacks on them and other websites.
The world faces a rush into approaches such as “Von Neumann architectures” and “AgenticAI” frameworks that are reportedly capable of, or soon will enable, computers to reprogram themselves. These computer programs are supposedly protected against runaway functions, but the [OpenAI](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/openai/) incident seems to have put that to rest forever.
We are in the middle ground between machine learning and actual artificial intelligence, which would require that AI becomes self-aware and pursues its own goals.
The [ChatGPT](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/chatgpt/) incident with [Hugging Face](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/hugging-face/) proves – as if proof were even necessary – that AI can and will go beyond human control whenever it can. That means, in military terms, fully autonomous weapons that will decide whether and when to kill people.
Drones and a variety of other weapon systems can identify and pick targets for destruction.
But there is hope that our and our adversaries’ computer researchers, including those at [OpenAI](https://www.washingtontimes.com/topics/openai/), will find a way to keep humans in the driver’s seat.
